442.title: Ashtpadi 2, salok: destroyer of pain
442.hook: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa: He destroys the pain of the humble (Sukhmani 2)
442.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the second ashtpadi, and some say it, or the whole bani, for someone who is ill or suffering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat, and your line: begin with remembering. Today, the second ashtpadi opens.

There's a kind of pain that doesn't make the news. The person who lost their job and hasn't told anyone yet. The old man whose children call twice a year. The new immigrant who can't read the letters arriving in the mail. Nobody stands up for them. They don't have someone to ring, a cousin who knows someone, a name that opens doors. In Guru Arjan's Punjab there were words for people like that, and the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens by naming them, and who stands with them.
screen: `PAIN THAT DOESN'T MAKE THE NEWS.` → `NO ONE TO RING.` → `ASHTPADI 2 NAMES THEM.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, ghat ghat naath anaath. Word by word. Deen: the poor, the humble, the ones with nothing to bargain with. Darad: pain, the ache that won't go away. Dukh: suffering, the opposite of the sukh in Sukhmani. Bhanjanaa: the breaker, the one who smashes it to pieces. So: the One who breaks the pain and suffering of the humble. Then ghat ghat naath: master of every heart, every single body. Then anaath, and here readers differ. Some translators take it as another name for God: the One with no master above. Others read naath anaath together: master of the masterless. In everyday Punjabi an anaath is an orphan, someone with no one, and on that reading the One protects those with no protector. The second line is Nanak's own voice. In paraphrase: I have come to Your shelter; God, be with Nanak. Notice two things. The salok doesn't say pain never comes. It says there's a breaker of pain, and names who the breaker stands with: not the powerful, but the humble, and on one reading the unprotected. And look where the Guru puts himself: not above the deen, but among them. He comes to the shelter too. In the days ahead, this ashtpadi walks into the hardest places a person goes, where no family can follow. But it begins here, with a name for God anyone in pain can call on: the one who breaks it.

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind whose pain you know about, or who you sense has no one to ring, and see them as clearly as you can. If you pray, say the salok's first words for them, deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, or simply Waheguru; if not, hold them in mind and wish them one thing: that the pain breaks, a little.
Dukh, suffering: Sukhmani's second section, whose salok names God the breaker of the pain of the humble and the master of every heart.
Your line: he breaks pain. And the Guru stands among the humble, not above them. Until tomorrow.

443.title: Where no family can go
443.hook: where no mother, father, child or friend can go, the Name goes with you (Sukhmani 2)
443.tomorrow: The Name on the hard road
443.howItsDone: Some Sikh families read this stanza, or the whole of Sukhmani, at the bedside of someone who is ill or dying.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dukh, and your line: he breaks pain, the protector of those with no protector. Today, the second ashtpadi's first stanza.

A hospital corridor, late. A family has walked with someone as far as they can: the parking lot, the waiting room, the double doors marked staff only. Then a nurse gently says, this is as far as you go. The doors swing shut, and everyone who loves the patient is on the wrong side. There are places a person has to go without the people who love them. The second ashtpadi's first stanza walks right up to that door.
screen: `A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR, LATE.` → `THIS IS AS FAR AS YOU GO.` → `THE DOORS SWING SHUT.`

segments.voice: The stanza begins, in paraphrase: where there is no mother, no father, no children, no friends, no brother, there, O mind, the Name goes with you as your help. The opening words are jah maat pitaa sut meet na bhaaee: a person's closest ties, named one by one, and set down at the door. Then the stanza goes into harder places still. In paraphrase: where the great and terrible messenger of death would crush you, there only the Name goes along with you. Where the difficulty is very heavy, the Name of God saves you in an instant. Notice what the stanza isn't saying. It isn't saying your family doesn't matter, or that love is useless. Sikh teaching honors the householder's life, the life of family and work. The stanza points at something plainer: there are rooms other people can't enter with you. The operating room. The last hours of a life. And, in the stanza's own picture, the meeting with the messenger of death. In every one of those rooms, it says, there is a companion who doesn't stop at the door. Read at a bedside, the stanza doesn't say the family isn't enough. It says the family can't go everywhere, and in the stanza's words, the Name can.
screen: `NO MOTHER, FATHER, CHILD OR FRIEND.` · `THE NAME GOES WITH YOU AS HELP.` · `ROOMS OTHERS CAN'T ENTER.` · `A COMPANION PAST THE DOOR.` · then, large: `THE NAME GOES TOO.`

segments.voice: Picture the people who walk with you as far as they can, and be grateful for each one; then picture a door they can't come through, and you stepping through it. If you pray, say Waheguru and imagine the Name stepping through beside you; if you don't, notice your own breath, which also comes with you everywhere.
Naam, the Name: the first stanza of Sukhmani's second ashtpadi, where no mother, father, child or friend can follow, the Name goes with you as your help.
Your line: the name goes too. Love walks you all the way to the door. Four hundred forty-three days now.

444.title: The Name on the hard road
444.hook: the Name helps on the long road where all else fails (Sukhmani 2)
444.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this stanza within the second ashtpadi, and some return to it during long illnesses, journeys and other hard stretches of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam, and your line: the name goes too. Today, the road on the other side of that door.

A long journey on foot: days of dusty road between towns, no signpost you can trust, no inn guaranteed. Before setting out, a traveler needs a tosaa, a bundle of provisions wrapped in cloth. Nobody sensible leaves without one. Sukhmani's second ashtpadi knows that world. It takes the traveler's bundle, the dark road, the burning sun, the stranger's town, and asks what you'd want with you on the hardest road of all.
screen: `A LONG ROAD ON FOOT.` → `A TOSAA: FOOD WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `WHAT DO YOU TAKE ON THE HARDEST ROAD?`

segments.voice: The stanza is a string of journeys, each with its own danger, and each answered by the Name. In paraphrase: on the road whose miles cannot be counted, the Name of God is your provisions. On the road of utter darkness, the Name of God is the light with you. On the road where no one knows you, the Name of God is there to recognize you. Where the heat is fierce and the sun burns, the Name of God is your shade. Where thirst torments you, the Name of God rains down like nectar. Five dangers: distance, darkness, being a stranger, heat, thirst. Every one gets an answer. The word for provisions is tosaa, the bundle from the hook. So the Name is food when the road is too long, light in the dark, a familiar face in a town of strangers, shade at noon, water when you're parched. Some readers hear this as the journey after death, the road the previous stanza began. Others hear it in life too. A long illness has miles that can't be counted. Depression can be a road of utter darkness. Moving to a new country is a town where no one knows your name. The stanza doesn't say the road will be shortened, or that you can skip it. It promises company on it, and provisions for it.

segments.voice: Think of one hard thing ahead, a long shift, a difficult call, a stretch of caring for someone, and pick the image from the stanza that fits it: food for the long road, light in the dark, a known face, shade, rain. Say that image to yourself slowly three times, adding Waheguru if you pray, and breathe with it, as if packing it like a bundle in cloth.
Tosaa, a traveler's provisions: in Sukhmani's second ashtpadi, the Name is food on the endless road, light in the dark, a friend among strangers, shade in the heat, rain in the thirst.
Your line: company on the road. The road stays long, and the bundle is packed. Day four hundred forty-four.

445.title: Living ashtpadi 2
445.hook: the Name as a companion, not a charm
445.howItsDone: Sikhs often read the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani with someone who is ill or grieving, and understand simran as remembering God in company with the Name, not as a spell to change outcomes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tosaa, and your line: company on the road. Today, living the second ashtpadi.

A lucky coin in a pocket. A charm hanging from a rearview mirror. A phrase muttered before a free throw. People everywhere keep little things that are supposed to make bad stuff not happen. It's easy to hear the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani that way: say the Name, and the bad thing goes away. But read it again. Not one of its pictures is about the road disappearing. The darkness is still dark. The heat is still hot. The door still shuts. What changes is who's with you.
screen: `A LUCKY COIN, A CHARM, A PHRASE.` → `SAY IT, AND THE BAD THING GOES?` → `READ IT AGAIN: WHO'S WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Gather the second ashtpadi together. The salok: the breaker of the humble's pain, the protector of those with no protector, and Nanak coming to the shelter. The first stanza: where no mother, father, child or friend can go, the Name goes with you. The road stanza: food, light, a known face, shade and rain. All through, the key word is sang: with, together, in company. The Name goes sang, with you. That's the difference between a charm and a companion. A charm is a tool: you use it to get an outcome, and if the outcome doesn't come, the charm failed. A companion is a presence: they don't stop the storm, they sit through it with you. Sikh teaching is wary of using sacred words as magic. Gurbani speaks sharply about empty ritual and outward show, as the next ashtpadi will show, and simran is meant to be remembering, not a spell. So when a Sikh family reads Sukhmani by a hospital bed, the hope is not mainly a bargain, read this and the scan comes back clear. The hope is that the person in the bed, and everyone in the room, isn't alone in what comes. That makes the Name for good days and bad ones alike. A charm is for emergencies. A companion is for every day: the commute, the kitchen, three in the morning.

segments.voice: Notice that you're alone with this lesson, or alone in your head even with people near, and instead of filling the quiet, sit in it and breathe slowly. If you pray, say Waheguru once, not to make anything happen, just to notice company; if you don't, notice that this moment is being lived, and you're here in it.
Sang, with, together: Sukhmani's second section in daily life, the Name not as a charm that stops the storm, but as a companion who goes with you through it.
Your line: never alone. The door still shuts, and someone still comes through with you. Four hundred forty-five, and counting.

446.title: Ashtpadi 3, salok: many scriptures
446.hook: I have searched many scriptures; none equals the Name (Sukhmani 3)
446.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the third ashtpadi; Sikh teachers cite it when speaking of the difference between scholarship and lived remembrance of the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sang, and your line: never alone. Today, the third ashtpadi opens with its salok.

Shelves to the ceiling. Notes in every margin. A reader with an answer to every question you could ask. A person like that can teach a great deal. And then there's the other kind: someone who has read very little, yet carries a steadiness the reader doesn't. A grandmother who knew three prayers by heart and lived every one of them. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Arjan, the author of Sukhmani, as the Guru who gathered the hymns of the Adi Granth. And the third ashtpadi opens with a surprising thing for a compiler of scripture to say.
screen: `SHELVES TO THE CEILING.` → `A GRANDMOTHER WITH THREE PRAYERS.` → `A COMPILER OF SCRIPTURE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok: bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol. Word by word. Bahu: many. Saasatr: the shastras, the learned treatises of Guru Arjan's world. Simritee: the smritis, the remembered law-books and traditions. Pekhe: I have looked at. Sarab dhadhol: searched through them all. Then the second line: poojas naahee har hare, Naanak naam amol. In paraphrase: they do not equal God, Har, Har; Nanak, the Name is priceless. Amol means beyond price, something no money could buy. Notice who's speaking. Not someone who dismisses books without opening them. Someone who says, I have looked, I've searched them all: a scholar, not a scorner. And what he found is that the books point beyond themselves. Learning can describe the Name, but it can't be the Name. Read this way, the salok isn't against study. The Guru Granth Sahib is itself a book, and Sikhs read from it and sing from it. The salok is about the difference between knowing about God and remembering God. Learning about water is not drinking it. Some readers hear the line as just as true of their own scripture: reading the Guru Granth Sahib without remembering the One it points to would miss the point too. Over the next days, the third ashtpadi's stanzas run through a long list of religious efforts, and set each beside the Name.

447.title: Beyond every pilgrimage
447.hook: pilgrimage, austerity and charity do not equal the Name (Sukhmani 3)
447.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite these stanzas of the third ashtpadi, and Sikh teaching draws on them to stress inner remembrance and honest living over outward ritual.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amol, and your line: nothing equals the name. Today, the stanzas that test that claim against every great effort.

You can run a marathon for charity, post the photos, and still be short-tempered with the person who drove you there. You can fast all day and spend it judging everyone who didn't. You can fly across the world to a holy place and bring your worst habits in the carry-on. Big effort outside, the same old self inside. The first stanzas of the third ashtpadi are a long list of big efforts. And they end with a short sentence.
screen: `A MARATHON, A FAST, A FLIGHT.` → `THE SAME SELF IN THE CARRY-ON.` → `A LONG LIST, A SHORT SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the list, from the first stanza, in paraphrase. Chanting and austerity, knowledge and every kind of meditation. Expounding the six schools of philosophy and the smritis. Yoga, rituals and religious rites. Renouncing everything and wandering in the forest. Every kind of effort: charity, burnt offerings, gifts of jewels. Cutting the body to pieces and offering it in the fire. Fasts and vows of every sort. Then the short sentence: none of these equal reflecting on the Name of God. Nanak says: through the Guru, chant the Name even once. The next stanza adds the picture behind today's title. In paraphrase: someone longs to die at a place of pilgrimage, yet pride and ego do not leave the mind. They wash themselves day and night, and the dirt of the mind doesn't leave the body. Notice what's being measured. Not whether pilgrimage or fasting is good or bad in itself. The stanza asks one question of every effort: does it touch the mind? Washing the body isn't washing the mind. A long journey doesn't automatically go inward. Guru Nanak said something like it in Japji: he would bathe at the pilgrimage place, if that pleased the One; without that, what use is bathing? So the third ashtpadi isn't against effort. It's against effort that skips the inside. The simple, sincere thing done with the whole heart outweighs the grand thing done for show.
screen: `CHANTING, FASTING, THE FOREST, THE FIRE.` · `NONE EQUALS THE NAME.` · `WASHED BODY, UNWASHED MIND.` · `DOES IT TOUCH THE INSIDE?` · then, large: `SIMPLE AND SINCERE.`

segments.voice: Pick one small thing you could do with your whole attention: make a cup of tea for someone and actually look at them as you hand it over, write two honest lines to a friend, water a plant slowly. Picture yourself doing it with nothing extra, not for anyone to see, and let the picture settle; if you pray, say Waheguru once.
Teerath, a pilgrimage place: Sukhmani's third ashtpadi says pilgrimage, austerity, ritual and charity do not equal remembering the Name, because washing the body doesn't wash the mind.
Your line: simple and sincere. The short sentence outweighs the long list. Day four hundred forty-seven.

448.title: The best of all ways
448.hook: the highest dharma is to repeat the Name and do pure deeds (Sukhmani 3)
448.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this stanza at the end of the third ashtpadi; its opening line pairs the Name with pure deeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teerath, and your line: simple and sincere. A week's end: the breaker of pain, the door, the road, the companion, the many scriptures. Today, what the third ashtpadi puts first.
screen: `SIMPLE AND SINCERE.` · `A WEEK: PAIN BROKEN, THE ROAD, THE SCRIPTURES.`

segments.voice: After a long list of what doesn't measure up, a reader wants to know: so what does? Yesterday's stanzas set fasting, pilgrimage, ritual and learning beside the Name, one by one. Stop there, and the third ashtpadi looks like a list of no. But it ends with a list of yes. The last stanza is a ladder of superlatives: of all the ways, this one; of all the efforts, this one; of all the places, this one. And its first rung holds two things together.
screen: `SO WHAT DOES MEASURE UP?` → `A LIST OF NO, THEN A LIST OF YES.` → `A LADDER: OF ALL..., THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: It begins: sarab dharam meh sresht dharam, har ko naam jap nirmal karam. Sarab: all. Dharam: a way of right living, a duty, a practice. Sresht: highest, best. So: of all ways of right living, the highest is to chant the Name of God and do pure deeds. Nirmal means spotless; karam means action. Here dharam is read not as a religion, an institution, but as duty, the way a person ought to live. So the line isn't a contest between faiths. It's a statement about what a good life is made of: remembering, and clean action, held together. Then the ladder climbs, in paraphrase. Of all rites, the highest is the company of the holy, which washes away evil thinking. Of all efforts, the best is to chant the Name of God, always. Of all speech, the nectar is to hear God's praise and speak it with your tongue. Of all places, the highest is the heart in which the Name of God dwells. Notice where the ladder ends. Not in a temple, not on a mountain: in a heart. After yesterday's pilgrimages, the best place turns out to be the one you carry around. And notice what's paired with the Name at the very top: nirmal karam, pure deeds. Remembering alone isn't the whole of it. It has to show up in what you do.
screen: `SARAB DHARAM: OF ALL WAYS OF LIVING.` · `THE NAME, AND SPOTLESS ACTION.` · `HOLY COMPANY, GOD'S PRAISE.` · `THE HIGHEST PLACE: A HEART.` · then, large: `NAME AND PURE DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Pure here means clean: no angle, no audience, no score kept. Let one such deed come to mind, a compliment you mean, something borrowed and returned, litter no one will thank you for, and picture doing it simply. If you pray, say Waheguru once, letting the Name and the deed sit side by side.

Dharam, right living: the last stanza of Sukhmani's third ashtpadi says, of all ways of right living, the highest is to chant the Name and do pure deeds, and the highest place is a heart where the Name lives.
Your line: name and pure deeds. No angle, no audience, no score kept. A week, gathered.

chat.says: Is that line about the highest dharam saying one religion beats the others?
options: No: dharam here means right living, and the highest is to chant the Name and do pure deeds.
Yes: it ranks the world's faiths and puts one of them at the top of the list.
No: it says chanting the Name alone is enough, and deeds don't really matter at all.
chat.meaning: Sarab dharam meh sresht dharam: of all ways of right living, the highest is the Name with nirmal karam, spotless action.

dharam.meaning: right living, duty; not, here, a religion
